title: White hake (Urophycis tenuis)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
White hake are a common groundfish species in the Gulf of Maine, which is warming faster than most of the world’s oceans (Pershing et al. 2021). In response to warming in the Gulf of Maine, white hake show a preference for narrow temperature (9-13°C) and depth (55-100 m) ranges and display a gradual northward movement in their center of gravity (LaFreniere et al. 2023). Nye et al. (2009) observed a range contraction in white hake in the Gulf of Maine. White hake may be affected by changes in circulation patterns. Small white hake larvae have been collected in early summer in a Gulf Stream warm core ring seaward of southern Scotian Shelf and southeast of Georges Bank. Patterns of strong recruitment have been linked to the strength of the Labrador Current on the Great Banks and strong onshore transport and downwelling conditions in coastal Newfoundland (Han and Kulka 2008) (Ings, Gregory, and Schneider 2008).

title: White hake (Urophycis tenuis)
text:
Life History Synopsis
White hake are a groundfish species inhabiting deep water from Newfoundland to the Mid-Atlantic Bight (Chang, Morse, and Berrien 1999). Males reach maturity at 2.5 years and females at 2.8 years; both males and females have a lifespan of around 20 years of age (Northeast Fisheries Science Center 2013). In the Gulf of Maine, white hake of all ages tend to migrate inshore in warmer months and disperse into deeper waters in colder months, while hake in the south move offshore to spawn in the spring; fall movements may be linked to prey movements (Langton, Pearce, and Gibson 1994). Based on the distribution and abundance of pelagic juveniles, as well as circulation patterns throughout the region, Fahay and Able (1989) suggested that the southern portion of the stock (below the Gulf of St. Lawrence) spawns in early spring (April-May) in deep waters along the continental slope, primarily off southern Georges Bank and the Mid-Atlantic Bight. White hake eggs are buoyant, and hatch in the water column in 3-7 days (Fahay 1983). Larvae may be affected by oceanographic conditions like warm core rings, the Gulf Stream, and Labrador Current for transport (Han and Kulka 2008) (Ings, Gregory, and Schneider 2008). White hake prefer temperatures between 7-20°C (Chang, Morse, and Berrien 1999). Eggs, larvae, and early juveniles are pelagic; older juveniles and adults are demersal. Most catches occur in Canadian waters at depths between 175 to 375 m with no differences between mature and immature hake. In the Gulf of Maine, depth preferences are 55-100 m (Fahay and Able 1989) (Nozères et al. 2015). Juvenile white hake settle to the bottom at around 2 months of age. Pelagic juveniles are in the upper water column during the daytime. Demersal juveniles inhabit muddy and fine grained sandy bottom sediment (Chang, Morse, and Berrien 1999) (Fahay and Able 1989). Demersal juveniles feed primarily on polychaetes, shrimps, and other crustaceans (Bowman 1981). Adults feed on fish, including juveniles of their own and similar species (silver hake), Atlantic herring, Gulf Stream flounder, and possibly alewife, shrimps, krill, and other crustaceans (Langton, Pearce, and Gibson 1994) (Nozères et al. 2015). The white hake fishery is managed as a single stock by the New England Fisheries Management Council, under the Northeast Multispecies (Small-Mesh) Fishery Management Plan. The stock is under a rebuilding plan, but is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Northeast Fisheries Science Center 2025).

Spawning occurs throughout most of the year (Able and Fahay 2010) (Cadrin et al. 2021), but relies on cold bottom temperature (8.5-13.5 C) (Chang et al. 1999). Spawning occurs in estuaries and nearshore environments; estuarine water column habitats are considered highly vulnerable (Guyant et al. 2022). The stock status of the Gulf of Maine/Georges Bank stock is unknown. The southern stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2023a) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2023b)).

title: Windowpane flounder (Scophthalmus aquosus)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
Percent biomass of windowpane flounder in the Northwest Atlantic increases with changes in seasonality, from cold springs, to warm springs, to fall (Dunn, Moxley, and Halpin 2016). Increasing temperatures (> 7-10°C) have been shown to displace windowpane flounder (Bell et al. 2021). In New York/New Jersey Harbor, cold winter temperatures decreased windowpane abundance and overwinter mortality in small juveniles (Wilber et al. 2016). Overwintering success appears to be driven in part by temperatures, with extreme cold conditions resulting in high overwinter mortality of age-0 individuals. This likely has a larger impact on fall-spawned juveniles since resilience to extreme cold temperatures is size-dependent and fall-spawned individuals have less time to grow (Neuman and Able 2009). Individual windowpane have also demonstrated avoiding hypoxic conditions (Cadrin et al. 2021).

title: Windowpane flounder (Scophthalmus aquosus)
text:
Life History Synopsis
Windowpane flounder inhabit shallow waters from the Gulf of St. Lawrence to Florida, but are most abundant from Georges Bank to Chesapeake Bay (Chang et al. 1999). They reach maturity around 1.5 years of age and can live up to 8 years (Cadrin et al. 2021). Windowpane spawn from February to November on the inner continental shelf, Georges Bank, and within estuaries. Spawning occurs in the Mid-Atlantic Bight in both spring and fall, whereas spawning in Georges Bank peaks in summer (Able and Fahay 2010) (Cadrin et al. 2021). Windowpane spawn in the evening or at night on or near bottom at temperatures ranging from 6-21°C (Chang et al. 1999). Eggs hatch after 8 days. The duration of the larval stage is unknown, but eggs and larvae remain in the water column feeding on suspended copepods (Chang et al. 1999). Surveys from Canadian waters suggest that small (< 10 cm TL) windowpane consume bay shrimp and crab larvae, which may be a transition point from zooplankton prey to larger prey items (Hanson and Wilson 2014). Larvae settle to the bottom at approximately 10 mm TL. However, individuals collected on Georges Bank may be planktonic up to 20 mm. There is no indication that settlement is driven by environmental factors (Morse and Able 1995). Juveniles that settle in shallow inshore waters move to deeper offshore waters as they grow. Juveniles inhabiting Georges Bank (< 60 m) undergo seasonal movements to deeper waters along the southern flank of the Bank occur during late autumn, as bottom temperatures drop, and overwintering occurs in deeper areas until late spring (Klein-MacPhee 2002). From Massachusetts to the Gulf of Maine, they can be found in estuaries and on the shelf (Chang et al. 1999). Adults are found on the benthos in waters < 100 m and tolerate a wide range of temperatures (0-26.8°C) (Chang et al. 1999). Adult windowpane may travel along the coast for considerable distances. Juveniles and adults may migrate to nearshore or estuarine habitats in the Mid-Atlantic Bight. Seasonal movements into offshore overwintering habitats have also been documented (Chang et al. 1999). Stomach content data collected during Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) bottom trawl surveys indicate windowpane feed on small crustaceans (e.g., mysids and decapod shrimp) and various fish larvae including hakes and tomcod, as well as their own species (Langton and Bowman 1981) (Chang et al. 1999). Windowpane flounder are managed by the New England Fishery Management Council under the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. The fishery is divided into two stocks: Northern Gulf of Maine/Georges Bank and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic. Overfishing and overfished status of the northern stock is unknown, as the assessment has not estimated reference points since 2020 (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2023a). The southern stock is not overfished and overfishing is not occurring (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2023b).

Sensitivity:








Figure 49.3: Winter flounder Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf





The Georges Bank and Gulf of Maine stocks of Winter Flounder both received Moderate sensitivity scores. Certainty for both stocks was 58%. For these stocks, five attributes had scores greater than 2.5: Complexity in Reproductive Strategy (3.3 and 3.4), Egg and Larval Survival and Settlement Requirements (2.7 and 2.9), Other Stressors (2.6 and 2.9), Spawning Cycle (2.8), and Stock Size (3 and 2.7) (Figure 49.1).
The Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stock received a High sensitivity score, with a certainty of 91%. Three attributes had scores greater than 3: Complexity in Reproductive Strategy (3.5), Egg and Larval Survival and Settlement Requirements (3.2), and Other Stressors (3.1) (Figure 49.1).
Winter flounder spawn in winter and early spring before waters reach temperatures of 6C (Pereira 1999). Spawning occurs in nearshore and estuarine habitats, including muddy and sandy substrates, and native salt marsh habitats which are considered highly vulnerable (Guyant et al. 2022). Larvae are dependent on bottom currents to help retain them in and around spawning areas and nursery habitats. Adults depend on estuarine habitats, which may be impacted by hypoxia and changes to freshwater inputs (Guyant et al. 2022). Predators include striped bass, spiny dogfish, and seals, which have all experienced distribution shifts that could result in increased predation pressure (Pereira 1999).
These results are similar to those from the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment where winter flounder were given a High sensitivity score. This score was also driven by Stock Status and Early Life History Requirements (Hare et al. 2016).

In the Southern New England/Mid Atlantic stock, mean exposure was High (2.66 +/- 0.72) (Figure 49.1). These patterns were driven by bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity exposure (Figure 49.5, Figure 49.4).
In the previous Assessment, winter flounder received a Very High exposure score (Hare et al. 2016). This previous score was driven by high exposure to sea surface temperature, air temperature, and ocean acidification (Hare et al. 2016).

title: Winter flounder (Pseudopleuronectes americanus)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
A number of studies describe evidence of changes in winter flounder growth, abundance, and distribution as a result of climate change. The Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic Bight stock declined sharply in the 1980s from overfishing, has not recovered, and is shifting northward (Able et al. 2014) (Langan 2021). Warm spring temperatures have resulted in poor recruitment (Able et al. 2014), and declining productivity due to warming estuarine waters has blocked recovery efforts (Bell et al. 2014). Elevated water temperatures can cause faster development rates of early life history winter flounder; length of incubation time is crucial as a nearshore and estuarine species as these areas are more susceptible to anthropogenic impacts (Klein, Smith, and Kritzer 2017). Increasing temperatures may alter predation rates, affecting survival of larval winter flounder, as well as migration and distribution patterns (Klein, Smith, and Kritzer 2017). In Narragansett Bay, warmer summer temperatures were linked to increasing mortality in young-of-the-year winter flounder. Greater abundance of mature winter flounder in the lower bay during spring may also indicate a potential shift in spawning migration timing (Langan 2021).

title: Winter flounder (Pseudopleuronectes americanus)
text:
Life History Synopsis
Winter flounder are found in estuaries and on the continental shelf from Nova Scotia to North Carolina, and are most common in the Mid-Atlantic north of Delaware Bay (Pereira 1999). They prefer temperatures between 0-20°C and depths less than 30m inshore and 100m offshore (Pereira 1999). The fishery is divided into 3 stocks: Gulf of Maine, Georges Bank, and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic. They reach maturity at 2- 3 years, varying across stocks with southern populations maturing younger than northern ones, and live to a maximum age of 15 years (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2011). Winter flounder spawn inshore in the winter through spring, peaking in February/March in the Mid-Atlantic and Southern New England and continuing into May in the Gulf of Maine (Pereira 1999). Timing of spawning aggregations is linked to inshore migration timing, which is complex and possibly related to time of year, temperature, lunar cycle, and photoperiod, as well as varying across years. Individuals migrate inshore in the fall, and migrate offshore in the spring. The Georges Bank population does not migrate (Pearcy 1962). Females deposit eggs at night and on bottom substrates, usually sand or algal mats, and can deposit multiple batches of eggs per spawning season (Ziegler, Zacharias, and Frisk 2019). Eggs are demersal and hatch within 2-3 weeks, depending on temperature. Larvae are initially planktonic but become more demersal as they metamorphosize, which starts 5-6 weeks after hatching. Larvae rely on bottom currents to keep them in and around spawning areas in inshore bays and estuaries. They are tolerant to a wide range of temperatures, salinities, and dissolved oxygen concentrations (Pearcy 1962). Metamorphosis is complete about 8 weeks after hatching, and is temperature dependent (Pereira 1999). Size, rather than age, tends to drive metamorphosis and settlement (Manderson et al. 2003). Larvae consume a variety of planktonic prey including nauplii, invertebrate eggs, calanoids, and polychaetes, with larger larvae consuming larger prey. Copepods and other zooplankton are important during metamorphosis (Stehlik and Meise 2000). Small medusae are important predators to larvae. Larvae can also be preyed upon by amphipods and Atlantic mackerel (Pereira 1999). Juveniles utilize marine and estuarine rocky, sand, and mud substrates, particularly fine sand and gravel as well as marine and estuarine water columns. They also occupy submerged aquatic vegetation, marshes, oyster reefs, and macroalgae habitats (Bigelow and Schroeder 1953). Juveniles consume a variety of prey including copepods, amphipods, and polychaetes. The diversity of prey increases and the importance of smaller zooplankton decreases with size (Pearcy 1962) (Pereira 1999). Adults are omnivorous opportunistic feeders. They feed during the day as they depend on sight to locate prey. Their diet is limited by mouth size; diets primarily consist of polychaetes and crustaceans (mostly amphipods), but also include bivalves, fish eggs, and fish. Diets can shift based on available prey (Stehlik and Meise 2000) (Pereira 1999). Predators of adult winter flounder include striped bass, spiny dogfish, and seals (Pereira 1999). The New England Fishery Management Council manages winter flounder in federal waters under the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. The Atlantic States Marine Fisheries Commission coordinates management in state waters. None of the 3 stocks are subject to overfishing. The Georges Bank and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stocks are not overfished; the Gulf of Maine stock has not been assessed and population abundance is unknown (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025b) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025c) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025a).

title: Witch flounder (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
There have been few direct studies on the effect of climate change on witch flounder. Larval growth and survival has been linked to temperature in laboratory conditions (Bidwell and Howell 2001). Murawski (1993) included witch flounder in a list of species that exhibit low variation in seasonal temperature or depth of occurrence. Mills et al. (2024) found that witch flounder distribution has actually shifted significantly toward more southern latitudes.

title: Witch flounder (Glyptocephalus cynoglossus)
text:
Life History Synopsis
Witch flounder are a long-lived flatfish species inhabiting deep, cold waters in the Northwest Atlantic from Labrador to North Carolina (Cargnelli et al. 1999). They are slow-growing, reaching maturity at 4.5 years for males and 6 years for females in Georges Bank and the Gulf of Maine (Burnett, Ross, and Clark 1992). Witch flounder can live up to 30 years, reaching a maximum length of 78 cm (Cargnelli et al. 1999). Witch flounder spawn from March to November, with peak spawning occurring in summer. The general trend is for spawning to occur progressively later from south to north. In the Gulf of Maine-Georges Bank region, spawning occurs from April to November, and peaks from May to August (Martin and Drewry 1978) (Burnett, Ross, and Clark 1992). Powles and Kohler (1970) suggested that witch flounder occupy three largely discrete ecological niches, resulting in the different life stages being geographically separated from each other. The pelagic egg and larval stages are spent in the water column over deep water. Egg hatching occurs 7 to 8 days after spawning, with the yolk sac absorbed 10 days after hatching. Larvae are pelagic, and the larval stage lasts from 4-6 months to 1 year (Cargnelli et al. 1999). Eggs generally drift southward, and shelf currents may transport some larvae. Length may be the biggest cue for settlement (Cargnelli et al. 1999). The juvenile stage occurs in very deep water when metamorphosed fish settle to the bottom. They are found over mud, clay, silt, or muddy sand substrates (Cargnelli et al. 1999). Juveniles remain separated from the adult population, occupying deeper areas until the onset of sexual maturity. Walsh (1987) suggests however that while the juveniles and adults are in different areas, the niche separation may not be true. Witch flounder are capable of inhabiting depths up to 1500 m, although the majority are found at 90-300 m (Martin and Drewry 1978) (Klein-MacPhee 2002). The main food items in the witch flounder diet are polychaetes and crustaceans, although mollusks and echinoderms are also important. Overall, polychaetes were by far the most important food item, accounting for greater than 70% of the diet (Maurer and Bowman 1975). However, there is a distinct ontogenetic shift in diet, with polychaetes increasing in importance and crustaceans decreasing in importance with age (Cargnelli et al. 1999). Adult witch flounder generally do not migrate, although they prefer to stay within temperatures of 4-11°C. Some subpopulations may move from shallower waters in warmer months to deeper overwintering waters. Migration was not observed in the Gulf of Maine (Cargnelli et al. 1999). Predators of witch flounder include monkfish, spiny dogfish, harp seals, Atlantic halibut, white hake, and some skates (Klein-MacPhee 2002). Witch flounder are managed as a single stock unit by the New England Fishery Management Council under the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. In the last Management Track Assessment, the stock status could not be determined due to a lack of biological reference points. The stock condition appears to be improving but is poor relative to historical levels (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2024).

Sensitivity:








Figure 51.3: Yellowtail flounder Sensitivity on the Northeast Shelf





The Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic and Georges Bank stocks of Yellowtail flounder both received Moderate sensitivity scores. Both scores had 88% certainty. These scores were driven by Stock Size (4 and 3.6), Spawning Cycle (2.7 and 2.6) and Egg and Larval Survival and Settlement Requirements (2.6). Adult Mobility (2.5) also played a role in the score for the Georges Bank stock (Figure 51.1).
The Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod stock of Yellowtail flounder received a Low sensitivity score, with 56% certainty. For this stock, only the Stock Size (2.8) attribute had a score greater than 2.5 (Figure 51.1).
Spawning occurs from mid-February to July on Georges Bank and in nearshore habitats in Southern New England and the Mid-Atlantic (Martin and Drewry 1978). Larvae feed on zooplankton prey and zooplankton abundance has been linked to recruitment success. Although it is also worth noting that studies directly testing for mismatches did not find evidence of mismatches between larvae and zooplankton overlap and recruitment (J. Kittel 2025) (Johnson et al. 1999) McManus and Richardson 2023). Larvae perform vertical migrations to help increase retention in and around nursery locations. Recruitment has also been correlated with circulation patterns and the Mid Atlantic Cold Pool. Both the Georges Bank and Southern New England stocks are under rebuilding plans (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025b) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025c).
In the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment, yellowtail flounder also received a Low sensitivity score. Similar to the Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod stock, the only attribute that scored above 2.5 in the 2016 Assessment was Stock Status (Hare et al. 2016).


Exposure:








Figure 51.4: Maps of each Exposure Factor for Yellowtail flounder. Exposure was calculated between 2014-2023 and 2025-2035





Mean exposure for Yellowtail flounder across its range was Moderate (2.34 +/- 0.89). Mean scores were also Moderate within the Georges Bank and Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod stocks (2.21 +/- 0.99 and 2.45 +/- 0.83, respectively). Average exposure was High for the Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stock (2.5 +/- 0.77) (Figure 51.1). Exposure was Very High over Georges Bank and High throughout most of Southern New England and along the coast of the Gulf of Maine (Figure 51.5). These patterns were driven by high bottom temperature, oxygen, and salinity exposure (Figure 51.4).
In the previous Assessment, yellowtail flounder received a High Exposure score (Hare et al. 2016).








Figure 51.5: Total Exposure on the Northeast Shelf for Yellowtail flounder. Total Exposure is calculated by applying the logic rule from Hare et al. (2016) within grid cells across exposure factors (see Figure 51.4)







Vulnerability:








Figure 51.6: Vulnerability on the Northeast Shelf for Yellowtail flounder. Vulnerability is the product of sensitivity and exposure (see Figure 51.5 and Figure 51.3)





Yellowtail flounder received a mean Vulnerability score of Moderate (3.96 +/- 1.88) (Figure 51.1). Scores were Moderate in the Georges Bank and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stocks (4.42 +/- 1.98 and 5 +/- 1.55, respectively). Mean Vulnerability was Low in the Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod stock due to Low Sensitivity (2.5 +/- 0.95) (Figure 51.1). Vulnerability was High over portions of Georges Bank, and Moderate over the Bank and in Southern New England (Figure 51.6). These scores did not change when exposure was calculated using only factors important to yellowtail distribution (Figure 51.1).
In the previous Assessment, yellowtail flounder received a Low Vulnerability score (Hare et al. 2016).

title: Yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea)
text:
Data Quality Metrics

Life History Data Quality:
Between 93 - 97% of data quality scores were greater than or equal to 2 across both stocks, indicating excellent data quality. Complexity in Reproductive Strategy was identified as a data gap (mean attribute data quality score < 2) for the Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stock (Figure 51.1).



Model Confidence Score:
The yellowtail distribution model received a 2.4 (+/- 0.2) mean model confidence score, indicating moderate confidence in the model. Experts noted that the model overpredicted distributions over Georges Bank, but otherwise accurately predicted distributions. The ensemble model AUC score was 0.88, indicating good model performance.

Additional Metrics

Distribution Shifts:








Figure 51.7: Distribution shifts on the Northeast Shelf for Yellowtail flounder. Polygons illustrate core habitat (left) and species range (right) for five-year average periods. Points illustrate weighted centroid, calculated as the average position with species distribution models as weights. Inset timeseries illustrate the shift in core and habitat range area over time. Circles represent points from the MOM6 hindcast; triangles represent points from the MOM6 forecast. Dashed lines represent significant linear regressions





Yellowtail flounder core habitat and range decreased significantly between 1993 and 2023. Core habitat loss occurred in southern New England and along the coast of the Gulf of Maine. Yellowtail flounder lost habitat at the southern edge of their range in the Mid Atlantic Bight (Figure 51.7). The distribution centroid shifted 11 km east-northeast.
Under near future ocean conditions, yellowtail flounder are expected to gain core habitat and ranges are expected to expand. Yellowtail flounder are predicted to gain more core habitat over Georges Bank. Ranges are predicted to expand southward in the Mid Atlantic Bight (Figure 51.7). The distribution centroid is predicted to shift 9 km southeast.
In the previous assessment, yellowtail flounder received a High Distributional Vulnerability Rank score due to high larval dispersal, moderate mobility, and variety of preferred habitats (Hare et al. 2016).

Directional Effect:
Experts predicted that the effects of climate change on Yellowtail flounder would be negative for both the Georges Bank and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stocks. Certainty for both stocks was high at 98% and 100% respectively. In the 2016 Climate Vulnerability Assessment, experts also predicted that yellowtail would be negatively impacted by climate change (Hare et al. 2016). For the Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod stock, the effect was predicted to be neutral, but with lower certainty (86%). Increased temperatures have been linked to decreased productivity, increased larval mortality, and reduced settlement rates (J. A. Kittel et al. 2026) (Klein, Smith, and Kritzer 2017). Recruitment has also been linked to the Mid-Atlantic Cold Pool (J. Kittel 2025).

title: Yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea)
section: Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
text:
Climate Effects on Abundance and Distribution
Yellowtail flounder abundance, distribution, and recruitment have been associated with a number of environmental and climate indices. Rapid warming of the Northwest Atlantic has resulted in decreased productivity in yellow flounder (J. A. Kittel et al. 2026). Higher temperatures can increase mortality in yellowtail flounder larvae, and faster rates of warming causing earlier stratification may reduce settlement rates in juveniles (Klein, Smith, and Kritzer 2017). Yellowtail recruitment in Southern New England is highly correlated with the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) and air temperature (Sullivan, Cowen, and Steves 2005). Low recruitment since 1990 was associated with unfavorable environmental conditions caused by a northward shift in the Gulf Stream (Xu 2016) (J. Kittel 2025). The Mid-Atlantic Cold Pool, bottom temperature, and the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) are also linked to recruitment (J. Kittel 2025). As warming continues, joint management between the United States and Canada may be more challenging as distributions change (Sumaila, Palacios-Abrantes, and Cheung 2020).

title: Yellowtail flounder (Limanda ferruginea)
text:
Life History Synopsis
Yellowtail flounder are found in the Northwest Atlantic from Newfoundland to Chesapeake Bay, inhabiting sandy bottom waters between 130-230 m depth (Johnson et al. 1999) and at temperatures of -1 to 18°C (Overholtz and Cadrin 1998). Previous research has suggested that fish live up to 17 years, possibly as high as 20 years, although fish older than 7 years is unusual (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2012). The fishery is divided into 3 stocks: Gulf of Maine/Cape Cod, Georges Bank, and Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025a) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025b) (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025c). Most females are mature by ages 2-3 (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2012). Spawning occurs from mid-February to July along the continental shelf waters of Georges Bank, northwest of Cape Cod, Southern New England and nearshore along New Jersey and southern Long Island (Martin and Drewry 1978). Spawning peaks from April to June in southern New England and late June to July in Canada (Berrien and Sibunka 1999). Laboratory studies show eggs begin to hatch 6-7 days after fertilization (Benoit and Pepin 1999). At sea hatching times range from 14.5 days at 4⁰C to 4.5 days at 14⁰C (Walsh and Morgan 2004). Eggs are pelagic (most at 10-90m depth), with movement limited to currents in spawning locations (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1975). Larvae move from the surface down to about 20 m, with larger larvae making longer migrations. This habit may assist in the dispersal of larvae because circulation at the surface transports the larvae further and is likely associated with feeding behavior (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1978). Larvae feed on zooplankton, particularly Calanus (J. Kittel 2025). Once larvae reach metamorphosis size (11.6-16 mm) bottom temperature (4-8°C) and depth (41-70m) are the most important parameters for determining settlement (Collette and Klein-MacPhee 2002). Juveniles utilize marine and estuarine sandy and muddy substrates, as well as estuarine and marine water columns (Collette and Klein-MacPhee 2002). Rotifers, copepods, and brine shrimp nauplii were fed to juveniles in laboratory studies (Benoit and Pepin 1999). Calanus copepods are considered a critical food source for larvae/juveniles (Purchase, Boyce, and Brown 2000). Amphipods (41% by weight) and polychaetes (38.5%) dominate the diet of adult yellowtail, but they also can consume cnidarians, small crabs and shrimps, mysids, cumaceans, isopods, univalve and bivalve mollusks, echinoderms, and sometimes small fish (Bowman et al. 1987) (Bowman et al. 2000). Similar to other groundfish, yellowtail may be impacted by increasing grey seal and dogfish populations and resulting increased predation pressures (J. Kittel 2025). Other predators of juvenile and adult yellowtail include spiny dogfish, skates, cod, hakes, and monkfish (Johnson et al. 1999). Minimal migration patterns show that Southern New England yellowtail traveled eastward during spring and summer and westward in the fall and winter as a result of seasonal changes in temperature (Smith, Sibunka, and Wells 1975). Recent tagging studies, however, show that individuals generally don’t move between stocks (Goethel, Legault, and Cadrin 2015). Yellowtail flounder are managed by the New England Fishery Management Council through the Northeast Multispecies (Groundfish) Fishery Management Plan. The Georges Bank stock is jointly managed by the Council and Canada, as the stock extends beyond the international boundary. The Cape Cod/Gulf of Maine stock is not overfished and not subject to overfishing (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025a). The Georges Bank stock is overfished but under a rebuilding plan; overfishing status is unknown (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025b). The Southern New England/Mid-Atlantic stock is overfished but under a rebuilding plan, but not subject to overfishing (Northeast Fisheries Science Center (NEFSC) 2025c).

Bottom temperature, salinity, oxygen, and aragonite solubility, in addition to net primary productivity were important dynamic drivers of yellowtail flounder species distribution (Figure 51.11). title: Methods Overview
text:
Overview
The CVA2.0 will take a semi-quantiative approach, using both quantitative and qualitative methods.

title: Methods Overview
text:
Quantitative Methods
Species distributions will be quantified using ensemble species distribution models, forced by environmental covariates from the MOM6 hindcast (1993 - 2023) and driven by fisheries dependent and independent datasets. These species distribution models will then be projected into the future using the MOM6 decadal and long-term forecasts to quantify changes in species distribution and their drivers.


Qualitative Methods
Species sensitivity will be estimated following similar methods to the original CVA. We will perform a literature review to update our understanding of important life history attributes and solict expert feedback on the most important life history attributes.


R Package
All analysis was conducted in R. An R package is under active development to ensure methods can be replicated. Vignettes will be available to describe the functions. Workflows are also being documented and will be provided in their own GitHub repository.

title: RPackage Overview
text:
An R package is undergoing active development to document the workflows and codes used to contruct the new Climate Vulnerability Assessment.
The package will have 4 major components:

Building the ensemble species distribution models
Estimating exposure
Summarizing sensitivity from expert scores
Calculating final vulnerability scores

The following pages provide a tutorial for the different portions of the package.

title: Species Narratives
text:
Data Quality Metrics
This section describes the Life History Data Quality and Model Confidence Scores. These scores quantify how confident experts were in the data provided that were used to generate the sensitivity (Life History Data Quality) and exposure (Model Confidence) scores. Model forecast data was not scored, as it was in the previous assessment, because forecast data received high data quality scores in the previous assessment. Both data quality scores were provided by the experts and range from 0 - 3. Following the original analysis, a score above 2 was deemed acceptable (Hare et al. 2016).

Life History Data Quality
Life History Data Quality replaces the Data Quality score for the sensitivity attributes. It was calculated using identical methods to the original analysis (average of expert-provided scores) and uses the same rubric (Hare et al. 2016).

Rubric used by experts to score Life History Data Quality






Life History Data Quality Score
Description




3
Adequate Data. The score is based on data which have been observed, modeled or empirically measured for the species in question and comes a from reputable source.


2
Limited Data. The score is based on data which has a higher degree of uncertainty. The data used to score the attribute may be based on related or similar species, come from outside the study area, or the reliability of the source may be limited.


1
Expert Judgment. The attribute score reflects the expert judgment of the reviewer and is based on their general knowledge of the species, or other related species, and their relative role in the ecosystem.


0
No Data. No information to base an attribute score on. Very little is known about the species or related species and there is no basis for forming an expert opinion (please use judiciously).





Model Confidence Scores
The confidence in the species distribution models used to quantify exposure was evaluated both analytically and with expert feedback.

Area under the Curve
Model confidence was calculated analytically using the Area under the Receiver-Operator Curve (AUC). This statistic quantifies how well models classify binary data. The models were built on MOM6 hindcast data from 1993-2019 and AUC scores were calculated on presence/absence data and model predictions from 2020-2023 to explicitly test how well the models predict future conditions, especially in data-poor years such as 2020. The closer the AUC is to one, the better the model did at predicting observed presences and absences.
It is important to note that the AUC is limited by the scope of the data used to calculate it (in this case, the spatial/temporal distribution of samples from 2020-2023). For example, the AUC may not reflect poor predictions of a species presence outside of its known range if the region is undersampled (Type I error). Therefore, we enlisted the experts to provide the additional Model Confidence Score.


Model Confidence Score
The model confidence score was modeled off of the original Data Quality metric (now called Life History Data Quality) (Hare et al. 2016). This score asked the experts to evaluate whether the final species distribution ensemble model results met their expectations based on their knowledge of the species and the life history data provided using the rubric below:

Rubric used by experts to score Model Confidence






Model Confidence Score
Description




3
High Confidence. The model highly accurately reflects the species’ realized niche. It captures fine-scale nuances, matches expert field observations, and handles environmental transitions realistically.


2
Moderate Confidence. The model aligns well with known distributions and environmental drivers. Most key habitats are represented, though there may be minor inaccuracies at the range edges or in data-poor regions.


1
Low Confidence. The model captures broad trends but has significant “noise.” Environmental drivers likely don’t reflect actual species needs.


0
No Confidence. The model fails to represent known species range. It predicts species in unsuitable areas or misses well-known core areas entirely.



This rubric was developed to mimic the Life History Data Quality rubric.

title: Species Narratives
text:
Additional Metrics

Distribution Shifts
Distribution Shifts were previously assessed using a subset of Sensitivity Attributes (Hare et al. 2016). In this analysis, they are quantified with the ensemble species distribution models.
Three metrics are calculated to help describe how species distributions shift:

Weighted centroid: the mean location of the species distribution. Species distribution model results are used as weights in the averaging to help account for habitat use. This is similar to the Center of Gravity metric used by DisMAP.


Core Habitat & Range Area: the area defined as core habitat and species range. Core habitat and range are quantified 50 and 95% Kernel Density Estimator (KDE), respectively.
Leading and Trailing Edges: the 95th and 5th percentiles of latitude (north-south) and longitude (east-west) edges of the species distribution. The difference between the leading and trailing edges, representing the span of the species distribution in degrees, is presented as the latitude/longitude range.

The provided map illustrates average species ranges using 5 year averages from the first and last 5 years of the hindcast data and the last 5 years of the most recent decadal forecast. The provided timeseries illustrate how a species’ core habitat and range areas change throughout the MOM6 hindcast and decadal forecasts.
In the online version of the narratives, an animated gif is also provided to illustrate how species distributions and the leading and trailing edges of these distributions shift through time in both the hindcast and forecasts.


Directionality
Directional Effect is consistent with the previous analysis: experts were asked to score how they left the species would be impacted (positive/negative/neutral) by climate change (Hare et al. 2016). Scores were provided using a tally system, and certainty was calculated using the bootstrapping methods described in Hare et al. (2016), similar to the sensitivity analysis.

Supplemental
Additional metrics and figures are provided in the supplement. The supplement currently includes the following sections:

Exposure Timeseries
Ranked exposures were calculated monthly across space. In the analysis described above, scores are averaged across months, using the species distribution model results as weights, to create a single average exposure map for each factor. Scores were also averaged across space to create a single score for each month. Averaging occurred over the species’ range and within stock units if applicable. Total exposure was then calculated across time using the Hare et al. (2016) logic rule.
Timeseries for each exposure factor and total exposure are provided in this section.


Exposure due to Significant Factors
The methods described above assume that all of the possible exposure factors will impact the species fitness/vulnerability in the future. However, this may not be the case. Therefore, we calculated total exposure and total vulnerability using only the environmental factors that played a significant role in the final species distribution model.
Variable importance was calculated using model-specific methods, scaled between 0 and 1 for each component model, and averaged across models according to component model performance. Static variables such as bathymetry, rugosity, and distance to the coast were excluded. An exposure factor was considered important to the species distribution if its average importance was greater than 0.1 (indicating that the factor explains at least 10% of the variance explained by dynamic variables in the final ensemble distribution model). A radar plot is provided illustrating the factor importance in the model.
This section describes the total exposure results across time and space when only the factors that play a significant role in the species distribution model are considered. Both maps and timeseries are presented.
